title: Talks a lot — the word does the judging
core: All of these say "too many words," and the fact itself is never in dispute. What separates them is the verdict smuggled into the choice: how harsh the speaker is being, and whether the excess is charming, tedious, aimless, or merely padded. They also split along a second axis — some describe a *person* who won't stop, others describe a *text* that won't end. Pick the wrong one and you accidentally compliment someone, or accuse a memo of being an old man on a porch.

words.nuance: The polite label — it describes a disposition (this person talks a lot) without saying the talk was trivial, padded, or off-point. Its fanciness is the whole joke: too formal to be innocent, so it reads as dry understatement rather than complaint.

The only one that can be genuine praise: it points at *ease*, not quantity — no groping for words, no stalling. Use it for the persuasive advocate or the effortless host; it says the speech works, and only faintly hints it may be hard to interrupt.

The captive listener's complaint, and the only one that indicts the *subject matter* as trivia — the digressions, the neighbour's fence. It carries an age stereotype the others don't: the porch, the train carriage, the person you can't escape.

The sin here is direction, not volume — a short ramble is still a ramble because it drifted off the point. Uniquely, it is content rather than confused, and its noun sense (a Sunday walk) is warm, which none of the rest can manage.

The verb of the set, and it needs a topic: you expatiate *on* or *upon* something, at an audience. It concedes real expertise and enthusiasm — the speaker knows the subject — while raising an eyebrow at the unrequested lecture.

Aims at the text, not the talker: the ratio of words to content, sentence by sentence. It's the coolest word here — an editor's markup on a contract or slide deck, faulting the padding while granting the ideas may be fine. (Software's *verbose mode* is neutral.)

Faults total length rather than per-sentence padding — the four-page memo that says no. It's the bookish, unmistakably disapproving upgrade of verbose, reserved for formal prose and set speeches, never for chatter.

exam_note: The trap is connotation-matching in Sentence Equivalence: *voluble* and *loquacious* can pair (talkative person, no sting), and *verbose* and *prolix* can pair (padded prose), but crossing the axes — garrulous with verbose, prolix with voluble — is always the wrong pair.
